newsitem.title: USA: Montana Freeman pleads guilty to bank fraud.
newsitem.headline: Montana Freeman pleads guilty to bank fraud.

text.p: A Montana man linked to the anti-government Freemen group that was involved in an 81-day standoff with federal agents last year pleaded guilty to bank fraud Thursday, prosecutors said.

Lavon Hanson entered the guilty plea at a hearing in U.S. District Court in Billings after reaching a plea agreement with authorities, the U.S. Attorney's office in Billings said. He was the first to plead guilty of 24 Montana Freemen and supporters who have been charged with various offences.

Hanson faced federal charges of submitting a fraudulent "certified money order" for $428,000 to the Farm Credit Bank of Spokane, Washington, in an attempt to pay off the loans of a neighbour whose property was being foreclosed.
He pleaded guilty to one count of bank fraud. Two counts of mail fraud were dropped, the U.S. Attorney's office said. Hanson will be sentenced Oct. 3 and faces a penalty of 18 to 24 months in jail.

Hanson was arrested on March 25, 1996, shortly after the arrests of Freemen leaders LeRoy Schweitzer and Daniel Petersen. The arrests marked the beginning of a tense 81-day standoff between armed Freemen and FBI agents at a remote Montana ranch. Hanson was not involved in the standoff, according to the U.S. Attorney's office.

The standoff ended peacefully on June 13, 1996, with the surrender of the Freemen who remained inside the ranch that they called "Justus Township." The far right-wing Freemen set up their own tiny republic at the ranch near Jordan, Montana, with its own laws, courts and white supremacist religion.
The government accused them of running a sophisticiated financial scam, writing fake checks and money orders that defrauded businesses out of at least $1.8 million.
Some Freemen have disrupted court hearings, refusing to accept the authority of a federal judge.

Hanson was originally charged with conspiring to transport a fraudulent financial instrument, a "comptroller warrant" for $3,000,000, to California in an attempt to obtain cash to return to Schweitzer at the Freemen compound in Montana. That indictment was dismissed by the U.S. government and replaced with a new indictment earlier this year.
Hanson was convicted in 1991 of filing false tax returns that claimed multi-million-dollar tax refunds. He served 13 months in federal prison for that conviction.

Two other defendants, Casey Clark and Stewart Waterhouse, are to go on trial Sept. 22 for their role in the standoff. Both are charged with assisting federal fugitives to resist arrest. No trial dates have been set for any of the other defendants who face charges in connection with the standoff or other alleged illegal activities.
Twenty of the 24 defendants remain in custody awaiting trial, the U.S. Attorney's office said. Hanson was one of four defendants who had been released on bail.
